extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; scholars of epistemology; readers of John Locke
extracted.subtask_description: An exposition of John Locke's account of the origin, nature, and division of ideas: simple vs. complex, sources (sensation and reflection), and key exemplar ideas (solidity, pleasure/pain, existence, power, succession). Useful for understanding early modern empiricist epistemology.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ideas but from Sensation and Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: "No ideas but from Sensation and Reflection, evident, if we observe Children." — All ideas originate only from sensation (external impressions) or reflection (the mind's operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues from observation (e.g., children and newborns) that the soul does not think before the senses supply ideas; ideas increase with sensory experience and reflection. Example: infants largely lack reasoning because they lack impressions. Use this principle to judge whether an idea is original or derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind thinks in proportion to experiential matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mind thinks in proportion to the matter it gets from experience to think about." — The amount and activity of thinking depend on how much sensory material the mind has received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a child's development: as sensory impressions increase, the mind 'comes to be more and more awake' and can exercise higher faculties (remembering, imagining, reasoning). This is an empirical criterion for cognitive development and the richness of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: A man begins to have ideas when he first has sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: "WHEN HE FIRST HAS ANY SENSATION." — Ideas in the understanding are coeval with sensation; sensation is an impression or motion in the body noticed by the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke defines the temporal origin of ideas as the first sensation. To evaluate claims about innate ideas, test whether the idea could exist prior to any sensory impression or reflective operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original of all our Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "The impressions then that are made on our sense... and its own operations about these impressions... are the original of all knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All knowledge springs from impressions by external objects or from reflection on the mind's operations. Use this as a foundational criterion: any purported knowledge must be traceable to sensation or reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding is passive in reception of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the Reception of simple Ideas, the Understanding is for the most part passive." — The mind cannot refuse, alter, or obliterate simple ideas when they are offered by the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the mind is like a mirror that must take in impressions. This limits the agentive power of the understanding regarding the origination of simple ideas; use it to critique claims that simple ideas are fabricated by pure intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Simple and Complex Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some of them, are SIMPLE and some COMPLEX." — Simple ideas are uncompounded, uniform appearances in the mind; complex ideas are formed by compounding simple ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether an idea is elementary (simple) or constructed (complex). Complex ideas are analyzed into component simple ideas; this distinction underlies Locke's account of concept formation and combinatorial creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind cannot invent or destroy simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Mind can neither make nor destroy them." — No power of thought can invent a new simple idea not received by sensation or reflection, nor erase an existing simple idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test imaginative claims by asking whether anyone lacking the relevant sensory access could conjure the simple idea (e.g., a blind person imagining color). If not, the idea cannot be produced by understanding alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only sensory-affecting qualities are imaginable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Only the qualities that affect the senses are imaginable." — We cannot imagine qualities beyond those our senses (as commonly counted) apprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a constraint on speculative metaphysics: if a proposed quality would not affect any sense (as humans have them), it is beyond our imaginative conception. Locke allows for the possibility of other creatures with more senses, but that does not expand human imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of simple ideas by source
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas are divisible by how they enter the mind: (1) by one sense only, (2) by more senses than one, (3) from reflection only, (4) by all ways of sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify any simple idea according to its entry route(s). Examples: color (one sense), extension/figure/motion (sight and touch), perception/willing (reflection), pleasure/pain (both). This taxonomy guides analysis of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of one sense depend on functioning organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas which have admittance only through one sense (e.g., colors via eyes, sounds via ears) cannot be apprehended if the corresponding organ is disordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical test: if a sensory organ is impaired, the associated simple ideas will not be available. This informs arguments about sensory limitation and the contingency of certain ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Few simple ideas have names
rubrics_metrics.description: "Few simple Ideas have Names." — Many simple ideas (especially varieties of smell and taste) lack specific vocabulary and are instead denoted by generic epithets like 'sweet' or 'stinking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize linguistic poverty for many sensory particulars; lack of a name does not imply lack of distinct idea. Use examples (varied smells, tastes, colours, sounds) to show limits of language in cataloguing simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Solidity (impenetrability/resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity is the idea received by touch, arising from resistance that hinders one body entering the place of another: 'THAT WHICH THUS HINDERS THE APPROACH OF TWO BODIES... I CALL SOLIDITY.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's account includes subclaims: solidity fills space, is distinct from pure space, differs from hardness, and underlies impulse/resistance/protrusion. He gives experiments (pump, water in a sealed globe) to illustrate. Use the definition and distinctions when analyzing notions of matter and extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidity distinct from space and hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidity (repletion/impenetrability) differs from pure space (which has no resistance) and from hardness (cohesion of parts affecting ease of changing figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating physical concepts, do not conflate solidity with mere hardness or with empty space. Locke's distinctions are operationalized by thought-experiments and physical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas received by both sensation and reflection (pleasure/pain etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain simple ideas (Pleasure/Delight and Pain/Uneasiness, Power, Existence, Unity) are suggested by both sensation and reflection and 'mix with almost all our other Ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes the motivational role of pleasure and pain (they prompt attention and action), and treats existence, unity, and power as pervasive simple ideas. Use these to analyze motives, valuation, and metaphysical presuppositions in human thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain as motives and ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and pain accompany many ideas and serve as motives for action; pain warns and preserves bodily organs, but both can lead us to seek God as ultimate happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to psychological explanations: the presence of pleasure or pain attached to ideas explains choice, attention, and avoidance. Locke uses physiological and teleological examples (heat, light) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas of reflection: perception and willing (faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: From reflection we get ideas of the mind's operations, chiefly PERCEPTION (thinking) and VOLITION (willing); these constitute faculties called UNDERSTANDING and WILL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing mental phenomena, distinguish ideas coming from reflection (self-awareness of thought and will) from those coming from external sensation; anticipate later discussion of modes like memory, judgment, knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession is an idea suggested more constantly by internal mental trains: our ideas 'always... passing in train, one going and another coming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use succession to explain temporal awareness and the ordering of ideas; it's a simple idea derived largely from inner experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are the materials of all our knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "Simple Ideas the materials of all our Knowledge." — All complex ideas are built from simple ideas received via sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites scepticism about supposed innate simple ideas; instead, analyze complex concepts by decomposing them into simple components (analogy: many words from few letters; or complex numbers from the idea of number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive ideas can arise from privative causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even privative causes (absences) may generate positive ideas: e.g., the idea of a shadow/darkness can be a positive idea despite being caused by absence of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses this to explain how negative-named concepts can still produce clear mental content. Apply this when assessing whether an idea's external cause is a presence or an absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas in the mind are distinct from qualities in bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish ideas as perceptions in the mind from modifications of matter in external bodies that cause them; perceiving white or black is different from explaining physical particles that cause those appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating mental content with external reality. Locke stresses methodological separation: analysis of ideas belongs to the understanding, while causal/external investigation belongs to natural philosophy.
